meeting_header:
Date: 2026-09-12 | Time: 16:00 PDT | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Owen Lee (Redwood SE), Carmen Ruiz (Redwood CSM) / Leah Kim (Head of ML, Cartwheel), Samir Desai (CTO), Marta Lopez (Platform Eng), Evan Rhee (SRE)
summary: Intro discovery with Cartwheel Labs focused on time-to-first-inference (TTFI), pilot playbook for PLG/self-serve vs reserved Dedicated/private deployments, and initial security fit. Customer is evaluating hosted to accelerate dev sprint but has enterprise constraints around VPC and KMS for production. Agreed to run a short benchmark and pilot using Redwood free credits to validate latency and cost targets.
transcript:
00:00 Maya Patel: Hey everyone thanks for making time, quick roll call?
00:06 Leah Kim: Leah here, hi.
00:08 Samir Desai: Samir on from Cartwheel.
:11 Owen Lee: Owen from Redwood.
00:15 Marta Lopez: Marta.
00:17 Carmen Ruiz: Carmen.
00:20 Maya Patel: Great. Ok quick agenda — understand your current stack, goals for a first sprint to production, constraints (privacy/SOC2 etc), and show how our free credits + quickstart gets you to first token. Sound good?
00:35 Leah Kim: Yep that's exactly it. We're trying to figure if we should do hosted first to move fast or push straight to dedicated/vpc for security. Key metric for us is p95 latency under 300ms for short prompts and cost per 1K requests under $X-ish.
00:55 Owen Lee: Cool, couple clarifying q's — when you say short prompts are we talking ~64 tokens or 128+? And what's concurrency's look like?
01:03 Samir Desai: Most user flows are small, like 40–80 tokens, but we also have occasional long re-rank and summarize jobs up to 2k. Peak concurrency on weekdays maybe 40–60 RPS; steady background inference around 5–10 RPS.
01:22 Owen Lee: That's helpful. For 40–80 token workloads our hosted instances with the right batching profile usually hit the latency targets; dedicated gives predictable throughput when you hit sustained 50–100 RPS. Private (VPC) is obviously possible but has a longer onboarding window.
01:40 Maya Patel: Quick note on credits — we can provision a PLG credit bundle so two of your devs can get access today; that'll cover the first sprint and a small benchmark. No commitment to start.
01:50 Leah Kim: Nice. What about data retention and logs? We need audit logs and control over retention for PCI-ish data.
01:58 Carmen Ruiz: We do SOC 2 and have retention controls; hosted retains request logs for configurable windows and we can run a private pilot if you need customer-managed KMS and no logs leaving VPC. I'll attach our security pack after.
02:10 Marta Lopez: If we go hosted for the sprint what's the plan when we go to production? Would we need to rewrite code?
02:16 Owen Lee: Minimal changes. Same Redwood API surface across hosted, dedicated, private. Usually it's config/endpoint swap and credentials changes — we keep SDK/REST compatibility. There can be networking/setup steps for VPC peering but your application code and prompts remain unchanged.
02:32 Evan Rhee: On the dedicated side we care about autoscaling policies and pre-warm behavior; we can't have cold-starts for critical flows.
02:39 Owen Lee: Dedicated has warm pool options and autoscale policies we can tune — we also support burst capacity for traffic spikes. For critical flows we recommend a hybrid routing policy: primary to dedicated, fallback to hosted for overflow.
02:55 Leah Kim: Can you talk about cost tradeoffs? We ran some numbers internally and dedicated is a big commit.
03:01 Maya Patel: Totally — hosted is opex and best for early experimentation and PLG; dedicated/reserved is CAPEX-like committed discount and predictable unit cost if you have steady throughput. Redwood Optimize will give suggestions on batching and quantization to reduce token cost too.
03:18 Samir Desai: We also need SSO/SAML and RBAC mapping for teams.
03:22 Carmen Ruiz: We integrate with SSO/SAML and SCIM; RBAC is plumbed through the Console and also supports token-level scoping.
03:32 Leah Kim: Ok great. For the quickstart benchmark what do you need from us?
03:36 Owen Lee: A small sample of representative prompts (anonymized), a target latency SLA, concurrency profile, and access for two devs. We'll also set up a test harness (we can share a JMeter/postman script or a simple python harness).
03:50 Leah Kim: We'll share that. One more security question — KMS/HSM options?
03:55 Carmen Ruiz: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS integration and HSM options for on-prem. For hosted we use envelope encryption and can integrate with customer KMS for Dedicated Private when on a private plane. I'll include the KMS section in the security packet.
04:14 Maya Patel: Great. Quick demo of the flow — sign up, claim credits, and run a sample call. Owen can walk through a small example and the SDK.
04:22 Owen Lee: Sure. (demo noise) So you sign up, go to Console -> Credits -> Claim the trial bundle; then you get API keys scoped to the credits. From there it's a one-request call to /v1/generate. Example snippet: curl -H Authorization: Bearer <key> ... returns streaming. For the sprint we get you a dedicated sandbox model mapping so your devs won't compete with other tenants.
04:47 Samir Desai: How about emphemeral keys for CI?
04:49 Owen Lee: We support short-lived tokens and token rotation via the Console and API.
04:54 Leah Kim: What about model choices and quant? We want cheaper per-token for bulk summarization jobs.
05:00 Owen Lee: We have curated model versions and recommendations; for bulk jobs we often suggest lower precision / quantized variants and batch-config changes. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload.
05:14 Marta Lopez: On the network front, our security team requires VPC peering in prod — can we do a hosted sprint and then VPC a month later?
05:22 Maya Patel: Yes, that's a common path. Hosted quickstart for TTFT, then a short project for VPC peering and private deployment when you commit to capacity. We'll map the timeline in the pilot plan.
05:32 Evan Rhee: Timeline — if we claim credits today when can we run the benchmark?
05:36 Owen Lee: We can provision credits same day, get two dev seats, and the benchmark can start after we receive prompt sets — typically within 48–72 hours.
05:45 Samir Desai: Ok sounds good. Any regulatory concerns for EU data residency? We operate EMEA but primarily US for now.
05:52 Carmen Ruiz: We have region-specific hosting and can route requests to EU regions with data residency controls. If you need explicit contractual guarantees we'll surface that.
06:02 Leah Kim: Cool. I have one technical deep dive — how does your runtime handle KV cache for chat-like flows? We need short-term memory at low latency.
06:10 Owen Lee: We have automatic KV cache management and efficient attention kernels; for chat we keep KV in memory and only persist to cache store on checkpoints. Sometimes transcription shows K-V cash in notes which is a mishear. Latency is optimized by preferring in-GPU KV where possible and spilling to fast NVMe if needed.
06:30 Leah Kim: Makes sense. Any pitfalls you see with our pattern?
06:34 Owen Lee: Biggest thing is prompt distribution and cold-starts — pick a small set of production prompts for the benchmark and ensure the batching window matches your p95 goals. We'll outline batching config in the perf checklist.
06:48 Maya Patel: Ok wrap-up — recap: Redwood to send pricing + security pack + benchmark plan; Cartwheel to accept credits and share prompts/traffic profile; schedule 60-minute benchmark session next week.
06:59 Samir Desai: Thanks we'll get the artifacts over.
07:02 Leah Kim: Thanks everyone.
07:05 Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up.
07:10 (call ends)
